Question: Let \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) be circles of radius \(1\) that are in the same plane and tangent to each other. How many circles of radius \(3\) are in this plane and tangent to both \(C_1\) and \(C_2?\)
Solution:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be the centers of the two unit circles. Distinct tangent circles of equal radius touch externally, so \(AB=2\).

A radius-\(3\) circle with center \(P\) is tangent to a unit circle when their center distance is either \(3+1=4\) for external tangency or \(3-1=2\) for internal tangency. Thus each of \(PA\) and \(PB\) must be \(2\) or \(4\). We can count centers by these four ordered distance pairs.

If \(PA=PB=2\), then \(P\) lies on both auxiliary circles of radius \(2\) centered at \(A\) and \(B\). Their center separation satisfies \(0<2<2+2\), so they intersect at exactly two points. This gives two centers.

If \(PA=PB=4\), the auxiliary circles both have radius \(4\). Since \(0<2<4+4\), they also intersect at exactly two points, giving two more centers.

If \(PA=2\) and \(PB=4\), the auxiliary radii differ by \(4-2=2=AB\). These auxiliary circles are internally tangent, so there is exactly one center. Swapping the distances, \(PA=4\) and \(PB=2\), gives exactly one more.

These cases exhaust the possible distance pairs. They cannot count the same center twice because each center has one fixed ordered pair \((PA,PB)\). Each center determines exactly one radius-\(3\) circle, so the total is
\[
2+2+1+1=\boxed{6},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
